newsitem.title: USA: Study contradicts abortion, breast cancer link.
newsitem.headline: Study contradicts abortion, breast cancer link.

text.p: Having an abortion does not increase a woman's chances of developing breast cancer, according to a study of nearly 281,000 Danish women published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

The study provides reassurances to women who have had an abortion, especially after the claim last October by four U.S. scientists -- three of them vocal opponents of abortion -- that there was "overwhelming" evidence women who terminate a pregnancy face a risk of breast cancer that is one-third higher.

That study did not involve any original research. Instead, the investigators combined the results of 23 earlier studies involving more than 60,000 women. This technique, known as meta-analysis, is controversial because the conclusions can be influenced by which studies are selected for analysis.
In contrast to the October study, a National Cancer Institute meta-analysis of more than 30 studies released last February found no evidence that breast cancer is linked to abortion.

The new study gets around the meta-analysis issue because it is a direct examination of the vital statistics of all Danish women born from April 1, 1935, through March 31, 1978. Combining data from Denmark's registries for cancer and induced abortions, a team led by Dr. Mads Melbye of the Statens Serum Institute in Copenhagen found no difference in the breast cancer rates for women who had had an abortion and women who had not.

Patricia Hartge of the U.S. National Cancer Institute, in an editorial in the Journal, said the study "provides important new evidence to resolve a controversy that previous investigations have been unable to settle."
It demonstrates that "a woman need not worry about the risk of breast cancer when facing the difficult decision of whether to terminate a pregnancy," she wrote.

Although the Danish study did not confirm an abortion-breast cancer link, it did find that the small group of women who aborted after the beginning of their fifth month of pregnancy had a cancer rate twice the expected level while the cancer rate was slightly lower for women who aborted before their seventh week.
But it said the numbers were so small it was uncertain whether the results represent a significant trend or a statistical fluke. A larger study would be required to resolve that question.
